curriculum.lesson_evidence: Artists build pictures from three basic elements. Lines can be straight, curved, zigzag, thick or thin. Shapes are closed outlines such as circles, squares and triangles, and organic shapes with wobbly edges like leaves. Colour sets the mood: warm colours such as red and orange feel lively, cool colours such as blue and green feel calm. When you look at an artwork, name the line, shape and colour you see, then say what each one does for the picture.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
A drawing of a sunny beach has wide curved lines for the sand, a big orange circle for the sun and small blue triangles for sails. Name one line, one shape and one colour, and say what each makes you feel.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: 'The wide curved lines look smooth and relaxed. The big orange circle is warm and bright, so it feels hot and sunny. The small blue triangles look like sails on the cool water.' Each answer names the element and its effect.

WATCH FOR
Thinking that an artwork is only good if it looks real. Artists choose lines, shapes and colours on purpose to create a mood or idea, so a simple, bold picture can be just as skilful as a realistic one.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Choose a picture book illustration or an artwork at home. Write three sentences naming one line, one shape and one colour in it, and what each element does for the mood. Then draw a small picture of a quiet forest using only curved lines and cool colours.

Write a short reflection naming one artistic choice you changed and why. Movement or instrument work is optional, adult-supervised and can be described instead.

teach_steps.example:
WORKED MODEL
Example: a painting of a stormy sea uses thick zigzag lines for waves, large dark blue triangles for the water and a thin pale yellow curve for the moon. The zigzag lines make the sea feel rough, the dark cool colours add a gloomy mood and the small pale moon looks far away because it is thin and light.

teach_steps.explain:
Artists build pictures from three basic elements. Lines can be straight, curved, zigzag, thick or thin. Shapes are closed outlines such as circles, squares and triangles, and organic shapes with wobbly edges like leaves. Colour sets the mood: warm colours such as red and orange feel lively, cool colours such as blue and green feel calm. When you look at an artwork, name the line, shape and colour you see, then say what each one does for the picture.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner make intentional visual, music, drama or dance choices and name their effect, rather than saying an artwork is simply “nice”. Keep every claim linked to an element or technique.

One deliberate artistic choice with a named effect is more useful than a longer praise sentence.

Here is a more helpful example: Example: a painting of a stormy sea uses thick zigzag lines for waves, large dark blue triangles for the water and a thin pale yellow curve for the moon. The zigzag lines make the sea feel rough, the dark cool colours add a gloomy mood and the small pale moon looks far away because it is thin and light.
teaching.rule: Use an intentionally weak or disrespectful arts choice as a comparison. Name the specific error, then show a clearer or more respectful choice.
teaching.why: This helps the learner make intentional visual, music, drama or dance choices and name their effect, rather than saying an artwork is simply “nice”. Keep every claim linked to an element or technique.

teaching.feedback: The new example should use the same arts idea as the model, but with different content or material.
teaching.fix: Name the element or technique and its effect, not just decoration.
teaching.guided_attempt: Make or describe one fresh example that uses the same skill and write a short reason for your main choice.
teaching.misconception: Repeating the worked example cannot show transfer to a new artwork or performance.
teaching.model: Artists build pictures from three basic elements. Lines can be straight, curved, zigzag, thick or thin. Shapes are closed outlines such as circles, squares and triangles, and organic shapes with wobbly edges like leaves. Colour sets the mood: warm colours such as red and orange feel lively, cool colours such as blue and green feel calm. When you look at an artwork, name the line, shape and colour you see, then say what each one does for the picture. Now choose a different subject or piece to show you can transfer the idea.
teaching.rule: Use the same arts idea in a new artwork, song, drama or dance, not a copy of the example. Review clarity, safety and respectful practice.
